cells.text: A systematic estimation error relative to a defined statistical target. It is neither necessary nor sufficient for social unfairness.
A structural preference that makes learning and generalization possible, such as locality, smoothness, sparsity, or architectural priors.
Stereotyping, denigration, erasure, or asymmetric portrayal that changes how groups are represented rather than directly allocating a resource.
A difference in access to opportunity, service, exposure, cost, review, or another consequential resource.
A systematic mismatch between a recorded proxy or label and the construct the application intends to reason about.
A value judgment about which differences are relevant, acceptable, compensable, or unjust.
Protects parity of positive decision rates, but can conflict with differences in base rates and says little about individual evidence.
Protects parity of error behavior conditional on the true outcome, usually trading against calibration when base rates differ.
Makes a risk score carry a similar empirical meaning across groups, but does not equalize error rates at a common threshold.
Asks that relevantly similar individuals receive similar treatment; the difficult part is defining a legitimate similarity relation.
Uses a causal model to ask whether an outcome would change under a counterfactual change of a protected attribute along specified pathways.
Focuses on evidence, explanation, appeal, consistency, and the legitimacy of the process rather than only output parity.
Probe stereotypical likelihood or representation, but may not predict allocational behavior.
Hold task evidence constant while changing a demographic cue; validity depends on whether the counterfactual preserves meaning.
Examines descriptors, tone, hurtfulness, omission, or framing over sampled outputs rather than a forced label.
Treats abstention and safety refusal as outcomes because unequal refusal can become unequal access to service.
Varies prompts, personas, conversation history, language, and adversarial context to measure behavioral robustness.
Audits position, style, self-preference, rubric sensitivity, and human agreement when another LLM performs evaluation.
Change what the system observes; useful for missing representation but insufficient when labels or objectives encode the wrong construct.
Change which errors optimization treats as costly; can improve worst-group performance while affecting calibration or average utility.
Change the conditional policy learned from instructions, demonstrations, or preferences; can also alter refusal and style.
Change prompts, decoding, self-checks, abstention, or post-processing without retraining; effects can be fragile under context shift.
Change evidence exposure, routing, thresholds, tools, review, and escalation; often the most direct place to control product-level harm.
Detects regression, drift, and unintended trade-offs after the intervention enters a changing environment.
The system may rank, summarize evidence, generate interview questions, or influence human attention; opportunity can be allocated at multiple stages.
Quality includes grading, tutoring usefulness, accessibility, language support, and the ability to contest an automated judgment.
Clinical relevance of demographic factors, proxy validity, uncertainty, access patterns, escalation, and severity of missed cases dominate generic parity.
Calibration, pricing, proxy variables, documentation, strategic behavior, and legal constraints interact with allocational fairness.
Procedural rights, explanation, appeal, record correction, and asymmetric consequences can matter as much as predictive accuracy.
Ranking and moderation determine visibility, exposure, and who has practical access to knowledge or an audience.
The harm, population, construct, metric, tolerance, and intended intervention are versioned together.
Model, prompts, retrieval stack, tools, thresholds, filters, memory, and judge versions are reproducible.
Public benchmarks are combined with product-specific counterfactual, naturalistic, multilingual, stress, and subgroup evaluations.
Refusals, escalation, quality, exposure, incidents, appeals, and sampled outcomes are monitored where lawful and appropriate.
Material model or product changes are linked to the evidence that was re-run, superseded, or invalidated.
Normative thresholds and policy choices are attributed to responsible institutions rather than presented as facts discovered by a model.
Represent mechanism hypotheses and distinguish legitimate from objectionable pathways rather than relying only on correlation.
Detect when the deployment environment moves outside the region for which fairness evidence was obtained.
Represent legitimate value variation explicitly while maintaining non-negotiable legal and safety constraints.
Place inspectable invariants, provenance requirements, prohibited-feature rules, or escalation conditions around learned components.
Use models to expand test coverage and analyze traces, while validating consequential findings independently.
Treat fairness as a monitored state with interventions and re-evaluation rather than a permanent certificate.
